Empirical support is strong across three datasets with consistent SOTA gains (Table 1), real-time throughput with a lightweight model (Table 2), and comprehensive ablations that justify core design choices: SAM/TAD contributions (Table 3, Table 6), prediction-source selection (Table 4), and the majority-voting threshold (Table 5). Minor concerns include notable per-dataset hyperparameter tuning (Table 12; Figure 5–6, 9–11), modest E-F1 on EPIC-Tent-O despite improved Avg-F1 (Table 1, Table 8), and a small trade-off in high-overlap localization (Table 11). Overall, the central claims—leveraging prediction inconsistency to detect both procedural and execution errors online, at real-time speed—are well supported.

A (summary): The paper tackles an important and timely problem—real-time, online error detection in procedural videos, including both execution and procedural errors, and supporting multiple errors per video (Section 1; Section 3.5). The main idea of leveraging prediction inconsistency between complementary detectors is novel in this context, and the concrete design—dual temporal branches plus robust/sensitive heads with SAM and TAD—is well realized and empirically justified (Figure 1–2; Section 3.2–3.4). The results are compelling: consistent SOTA across three benchmarks (Table 1) with real-time throughput in a combined setting (24.4 FPS, 18.8M params; Table 2), along with thorough ablations that attribute gains to the proposed components and the decision rule (Table 3–6). 

Limitations include notable per-dataset hyperparameter tuning for temporal ranges and TAD margin (Table 12; Figure 5–6, 9–11), and comparatively modest E-F1 on EPIC-Tent-O despite strong Avg-F1/C-F1 (Table 1, Table 8). Q5 (Strengths):
Q: Please give a substantive assessment of the strengths of the paper. Be specific, avoid generic remarks. This can, for example, include quality, clarity (e.g. well written), or significance, originality (e.g. a new definition or problem formulation, creative combinations of existing ideas, application to a new domain, or removing limitations from prior results.) If you have many, only list the least generic ones.
A (summary): 1. Clear, actionable core idea with novel operationalization. The paper turns “prediction inconsistency” into a concrete online error signal by pairing robust vs. sensitive heads and short- vs. long-term branches, then using a majority vote over four mismatch pairs (Section 3.5; Figure 1). This design directly targets both execution and procedural errors without needing ground-truth task graphs or LLM reasoning.

2. Method originality in sensitivity/robustness shaping. The Step Attention Module (SAM) uses action prototypes to stabilize robust heads (Section 3.2), while the Temporal-Aware Dynamic (TAD) module applies input-dependent affine transforms with a sparsity margin to amplify error sensitivity (Section 3.3; Eq. 3; Figure 2). The complementary roles are well-motivated and distinct.

3. Causal, online pipeline with an explicit decision rule. Training losses and inference steps are fully specified, including cross-entropy and smoothing losses (Eq. 1–2), causal mode filtering, and the mismatch-based voting rule (Section 3.4–3.5). The implementation is reproducible from the main text and figures (Figure 1–2).

4. Strong empirical validation across multiple datasets and error types. DUBAD achieves SOTA on EgoPER, Assembly-101-O, and EPIC-Tent-O (Table 1), covering execution and procedural errors. The gains are consistent across metrics (e.g., F1@10/25/50 on EgoPER; Avg-F1/E-F1/C-F1 on Assembly-101-O and EPIC-Tent-O).

5. Real-time efficiency with a lightweight model. The combined pipeline reaches 24.4 FPS with 18.8M parameters (Table 2), a practical improvement over LLM-based PREGO (1.33 FPS), and competitive despite the ensemble structure.

6. Thorough ablations that pinpoint what matters. The paper isolates the effects of SAM and TAD (Table 3), compares prediction sources for robust/sensitive votes (Table 4), evaluates the voting threshold (Table 5), and dissects loss components (Table 6). These analyses make the contribution attribution unusually clear.

7. Mechanistic evidence that sensitivity drives inconsistency on errors. Histograms (Figure 3) show sensitive heads dispersing probability mass across more classes on errors, and heatmaps (Figure 4; Figure 8) visualize feature sparsity/inconsistency induced by TAD during erroneous segments, connecting modules to behavior.

8. Demonstrated multi-error handling. Unlike prior online approaches that often stop at the first error, the majority-vote design over independent predictors naturally supports multiple and interacting errors within a video (Section 3.5; qualitative Figure 7).

9. One-class training yet robust deployment. Training exclusively on normal videos while attaining high E-F1/C-F1 (Table 1; Table 8) shows that inconsistency-based detection is effective without error supervision, addressing a key data-collection bottleneck.

10. Maintained action recognition quality in the robust heads. The robust detector retains strong temporal action segmentation performance (Table 7), indicating the method does not compromise standard recognition while adding error sensitivity.

11. Sensible temporal design backed by data analysis. The short/long temporal ranges are justified empirically with task-dependent action counts per window (Appendix Figures 12–15) and performance sweeps over s/l (Figure 6; Figure 9), supporting the dual-branch rationale.

12. Practical guidance via hyperparameter studies. The paper provides explicit sensitivity to β and voting thresholds (Figure 5; Table 5) and reports per-dataset optimal s/l/β/m (Table 12), which will help practitioners adapt the method.
Q6 (Weaknesses):
Q: Please give a substantive assessment of the weaknesses of the paper. Focus on constructive and actionable insights on how the work could improve towards its stated goals. Be specific, avoid generic remarks. For example, if you believe the contribution lacks novelty, provide references and an explanation as evidence; if you believe experiments are insufficient, explain why and exactly what is missing, etc. Unclarities are adressed later, so only list real weaknesses. If you have many, only list the least generic ones.
A (summary): 1. Heavy per-dataset hyperparameter tuning and unclear generalization of the recipe. The method’s effectiveness hinges on carefully chosen temporal ranges (s, l), TAD margin β, and the causal mode filter m, which vary widely across datasets and even tasks (Table 12; Figure 5–6, 9–11). This undermines plug-and-play deployability for real-time assistants. Actionable: (a) report a single default configuration that performs competitively across datasets; (b) add an automatic selection strategy (e.g., validation-driven or momentum-adaptive s, l; β learned per-branch via a constraint or regularizer); (c) include sensitivity curves when deviating from the “optimal” in Table 12 to quantify robustness.

2. Limited evidence on detection latency and responsiveness. The causal mode filter is causal but uses large windows (e.g., m=150 on EPIC-Tent-O; Table 12), which likely introduces seconds of decision lag, contradicting the emphasis on instantaneous feedback. No detection delay metrics are reported. Actionable: report time-to-detect/error onset lag distributions vs. F1 on all datasets; include ablations varying m (Figure 11) together with measured latency, and add a “controlled-delay” setting as suggested in the Conclusion to characterize the accuracy–latency trade-off.

3. Error detection on EPIC-Tent-O remains weak. Despite higher Avg-F1, the error F1 is low (E-F1=27.6% with E-Precision 28.6 and E-Recall 26.7 in Table 8), suggesting limited practical utility for detecting actual mistakes in this dataset. Actionable: analyze failure modes by error type and action duration; evaluate whether tuning s/l toward longer contexts (Figure 6) or adjusting β (Figure 5/10) can improve E-Recall; consider a learned combiner (instead of hard majority vote) that weights the four pairwise inconsistencies adaptively for domains with long actions.

4. Decision rule is hand-crafted and potentially brittle. The “≥3 mismatches” threshold is selected via ablation (Table 5) but remains a hard rule over argmax labels. This discards uncertainty information in the softmax scores that could capture near-misses or partial agreement. Actionable: (a) compare against probabilistic inconsistency measures (e.g., KL/JS divergence between distributions) and calibrated entropy thresholds; (b) evaluate a light meta-classifier over the four logits pairs to learn the decision boundary; (c) consider per-branch confidence calibration to avoid overconfident but wrong sensitive predictions.

5. SAM’s reliance on fixed action prototypes may hinder out-of-distribution robustness. The Step Attention Module (Section 3.2) uses averaged per-class prototypes from normal videos, which presumes a stable action taxonomy and consistent feature semantics. There is no analysis on drift (e.g., different camera/device domains) or unseen/rare actions. Actionable: (a) add cross-domain or cross-task transfer tests (train on a subset of tasks or subjects; test on held-out ones); (b) evaluate prototype robustness to class imbalance; (c) compare to alternatives such as instance-wise memory or online-updated prototypes.

6. TAD objective lacks a clear justification for “sparsity” and selection. The TAD loss (Eq. 3) constrains the norm of Hk but is not an explicit sparsity penalty; the link to feature selection is mostly empirical via heatmaps (Figure 4, Figure 8). Actionable: (a) report quantitative sparsity metrics (e.g., proportion of near-zero channels) vs. β; (b) compare L1 vs. the current margin loss for Hk; (c) ablate the GRU inside TAD (Figure 2) to verify the necessity of temporal conditioning in producing beneficial instability.

7. Missing comparisons to simpler or broader inconsistency/uncertainty baselines. The core claim is that “inconsistency” is an effective error signal, but comparisons are limited to PREGO/DTGL and internal ablations (Table 3–6). Actionable: add baselines using (a) disagreement between only short-vs-long branches without SAM/TAD; (b) stochastic inference disagreement (e.g., dropout perturbations) or small deep ensembles; (c) entropy-based thresholds on a single robust head. This would solidify that the proposed dual-branch robust/sensitive design is necessary.

8. No reporting of variability or statistical significance. All main tables (e.g., Table 1–2) lack variance across runs/seeds. Given the small gaps at higher overlap thresholds (e.g., EgoPER F1@50 is 23.9 vs. 20.9), reproducibility is uncertain. Actionable: report mean±std over multiple seeds; for EgoPER, provide per-task/error-type breakdowns with confidence intervals.

9. Limited quantitative evaluation of multi-error scenarios. Although Figure 7 qualitatively shows multiple errors in EgoPER, there is no event-level scoring that counts how many errors were detected vs. missed, nor fragmentation/merging analysis. Actionable: add a per-error event precision/recall on EgoPER (since Assembly-101-O and EPIC-Tent-O stop at the first error) and report over-segmentation/under-segmentation rates akin to Table 9 but at the event level.

10. Feature extractor dependence and fairness. For EgoPER, features come from TimeSFormer pretrained on Ego4D; for Assembly-101-O/EPIC-Tent-O, features are those used by PREGO (Section 4.1). This mixing may confound fairness and hides the impact of the detector itself across datasets. Actionable: (a) unify the feature backbone across all datasets (at least as an additional controlled comparison); (b) report results with a lighter backbone to demonstrate robustness to feature quality and better reflect wearable-device constraints.

11. Practical deployment claims not validated on target hardware. The Introduction motivates wearable deployment (e.g., HoloLens/Vision Pro), yet runtime is only measured on an RTX A6000 (Table 2). The large smoothing windows (Table 12) also suggest non-trivial latency. Actionable: provide throughput and latency on an edge device or with mobile-class GPUs/CPUs, and include memory/energy profiles.

12. Limited error-type breakdown on EgoPER. The paper asserts coverage of nuanced execution errors (Section 1; Section 3.5), but quantitative breakdown by execution error categories (e.g., addition, modification, slip) is absent; only qualitative examples are shown (Figure 7). Actionable: add per-category metrics on EgoPER to substantiate the claim that subtle execution errors are better captured than prior online methods.

# ABSTRACT
An efficient and accurate system for detecting errors in procedural tasks is crucial for supporting human needs in daily life, as it can provide instant notifications and guide people to correct mistakes. In this paper, we address the challenge of real-time and online error detection in procedural task videos by leveraging inconsistencies in action detector predictions. We propose a DUal-Branch Action Detector (DUBAD) framework, which integrates both robust and sensitive actions detectors. The robust action detectors generate accurate and stable action predictions, while the sensitive detectors produce inconsistent predictions when errors occur. To achieve this, we design a temporal-aware dynamic weight module that enhances sensitivity to errors using affine transformations with inputdependent, constrained weights and biases. Furthermore, we train the action detectors with varying amounts of temporal information to amplify inconsistencies in prediction when action sequences deviate from the correct order. For videos containing multiple or diverse errors, we apply a majority voting scheme based on mismatches between robust and sensitive predictions. Extensive experiments on EgoPER, Assembly-101-O, and EPIC-Tent-O demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in online error detection, while maintaining real-time efficiency with a lightweight architecture. 1

Error Detection in Procedural Videos. The research community has recently shown growing interest in error detection, which aims to detect the occurrence of or localize an action that changes the action sequence of a procedure or should not occur in a procedure. Specifically, among the offline methods, EgoPED (Lee et al. (2024)) determines the execution errors by thresholding the similarities between the predicted action features and input frames features. AMNAR (Huang et al. (2024)) generates action features conditioned on executed actions and follows the same strategy as in EgoPED for error detection. On the other hand, among the online methods, PREGO (Flaborea et al. (2024)) detects procedural errors by the difference in prediction generated by an action detector and LLM, with its strong reasoning capability to anticipate the next action given past actions. DTGL (Seminara et al. (2024)) learns the task graph from the training videos and detects an action as a procedural error if its preconditions in the learned task graph are not in the observed actions. However, existing online methods fail to handle execution errors or videos with multiple errors.

# 3.2 ROBUST ACTION DETECTOR WITH STEP ATTENTION MODULE (SAM)
We aim to develop action detectors robust to erroneous frames, enabling them to consistently produce accurate and stable predictions. To begin (see the solid arrow in the upper-left region of Fig. 1), the robust action detector of the short range branch f s processes a sequence of s frame features X s t = ( x t -s +1 , ..., x t -2 , x t -1 , x t ) ending at time t through a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), Gated-Recurrent Unit (GRU), and a linear layer as the classification head to predict the action logits a s t ∈ R P +1 at time t , where a s ∈ R T × P +1 denoting action logits after processing the entire video.

To enhance the robustness of the action detector, i.e., GRU s and Head s , especially when execution errors occur, we propose SAM to augment the features using action prototypes after MLP as an additional training input for the action detector (see the dashed arrow in the upper-left region of Fig. 1). The action prototype encodes the semantics of the corresponding action, guiding the detectors to learn generalizable patterns for action detector and produce stable predictions under errors. First, we generate the action prototype h i ∈ R D for each action i ∈ { 1 , 2 , . . . , P } by averaging over frame features corresponding to the action i in all training videos. We exclude background frames because background features are too diverse to be averaged as a prototype for feature matching. Second, we use a multi-head attention module (Vaswani et al. (2017)) to generate augmented frame features ¯ X s t corresponding to all frames of X s t , where the query is the frame feature x ∈ X s t , the key and value are the action prototypes h ∈ R P × D , where each row i corresponds to h i . See our supplementary material for implementation details. Finally, we feed ¯ X s t to GRU s and Head s to predict the action logits b s t ∈ R P +1 at time t with b s ∈ R T × P +1 representing action logits after processing the entire video. We follow this forward training process for f l with l frames to obtain ¯ X l t , a l t , and b l t . Notice that the difference in the input temporal range introduces inconsistencies in the predictions of the two branches when actions do not follow their expected sequences during inference.

To establish sensitivity (see the dashed arrow in the lowerleft region of Fig. 1), we build ˆ f s based on f s by additionally proposing the TAD module to convert ¯ X s t and ¯ X l t into temporal-aware representations that are more sensitive to erroneous frames. # 3.4 TRAINING LOSSES
DUBAD is trained on batches of frame sequences, each independently and randomly sampled from the training videos. Concretely, each batch consists of training pairs ( v, t ) from a random time t and video v . Next, we describe the training losses applied to the robust and sensitive action detectors.

Classification Loss. We adopt the same cross-entropy loss as in miniROAD (An et al. (2023)). The classification loss is computed only for the frame at time t while observing its k ∈ { s, l } prior frames. Additionally, we utilize a smoothing loss that minimizes the difference between two consecutive predictions in time. In particular, for time t of video v , let ¯ y v,t be the ground-truth action label, and p k v,t ∈ R P +1 be the softmax values computed from the action logits of any of the four classification heads of branch k such as a k or b k . The two losses for each sample in the batch are formulated below. For simplicity, we omit the video index v hereafter:

L k CE ( t ) = -∑ p ∈{ a,b, ˆ a, ˆ b } log( p k t, ¯ y t ) , (1)

L k Smo ( t ) = ∑ p ∈{ a,b, ˆ a, ˆ b } 1 P +1 P +1 ∑ i =1 ( log p k t,i -log p k t -1 ,i ) 2 . (2)

For each sample in the batch, the total classification loss L k cls ( t ) = L k CE ( t ) + L k Smo ( t ) is defined as the sum of the two losses for both the short and long range branches.

Temporal Aware Dynamic Loss. This is an auxiliary loss which is specifically designed to support the training of the sensitive action detectors ˆ f s and ˆ f l . As shown in Fig. 2, in order to compute the TAD loss, we formulate H s and H l by stacking ( H s t -s +1 , H s t -1 , . . . , H s t ) and ( H l t -l +1 , H l t -1 , . . . , H l t ) in memory for the short and long range branches respectively. This is different from the cross-entropy loss where the loss is only computed for the frame t . Consequently, we define the TAD loss for each sample in the batch as follows:

L k TAD ( t ) = max ( 0 , 1 2 D k -1 ∑ i =0 ( ( H k t -i ) T ( H k t -i ) ) -β ) , (3)

where D is the feature dimension, k ∈ { s, l } , and β is the margin that controls the sparsity of H k . Eq. 3 encourages H s and H l to select key semantic features of the frames. Furthermore, we use the same margin for the two temporal branches, i.e., H l and H s . As H l incorporates more frames, it tends to choose fewer semantic features than H s , leading to a different extent of error sensitivity for ˆ f l . Overall, L k TAD utilizes the temporal-aware and input-dependent design of the TAD to make the weights H k more sensitive to unseen error instances during inference.

Final Batch Training. To conclude, the losses of the two branches are added to derive the final loss L final ( t ) = ∑ k ∈{ s,l } L k TAD ( t ) + L k cls ( t ) which is further averaged over all sequences in the batch to train the robust and sensitive detectors.

# 3.5 ONLINE ERROR DETECTION DURING INFERENCE
At inference time, we process the video frame by frame from t = 1 to t = T to obtain predictions from the action detectors. We then 1) apply a causal mode filter, which only uses past frames to replace the action with the most frequent action within a window size m to smooth the predictions, and 2) perform error detection via action prediction inconsistency . First, we capture the inconsistencies in the following pairs: ( a s t , ˆ b s t ) and ( a l t , ˆ b l t ), where a s t and a l t provide correct or specific action predictions on errors, resulting in stable outputs. Meanwhile, ˆ b s t and ˆ b l t provide inconsistent action predictions on errors due to sensitive frame features ˆ X s t and ˆ X l t . Inconsistencies in the two pairs

# 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Dataset. We evaluate our proposed method on EgoPER (Lee et al. (2024)), Assembly-101-O (Flaborea et al. (2024)), and EPIC-Tent-O (Flaborea et al. (2024)). EgoPER consists of 5 tasks ( tea , quesadilla , oatmeal , oatmeal , and coffee ) with 386 egocentric videos and contains both execution and procedural errors. We use the given training/test split for evaluation. For Assembly-101-O and EPIC-Tent-O, which consist of egocentric videos with procedural errors in assembly domain, we follow the same training/test split as in PREGO (Flaborea et al. (2024)) and DTGL (Seminara et al. (2024)). Note that the procedure in each test video stops once an error occurs, meaning that only the last action is flagged as an error.

Evaluation Metrics. For EgoPER, we report the metric used in (Farha & Gall (2019)), the segmentwise F1 score under three overlap thresholds (10%, 25%, and 50%) based on normal and erroneous segments, denoted as F1@10, F1@25, and F1@50. They consider both localization and classification performance of error detection, especially for execution errors. For Assembly-101-O and EPIC-Tent-O, we report the same action-wise F1 scores as in DTGL for two complementary classification cases: erroneous → correct (E-F1) and correct → erroneous (C-F1). Their average yields Avg-F1. All F1 scores are computed based on predicted actions.

Baselines. We mainly compare our proposed method with two state-of-the-art online error detection methods, PREGO (Flaborea et al. (2024)) and DTGL (Seminara et al. (2024)) with direct optimization which performs the best in general. For EgoPER, we train PREGO with Qwen 2.5 (Yang et al. (2024)) as its LLM and DTGL from scratch with their public codes and evaluate their performance.

# 5 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this paper, we propose DUal-Branch Action Detector (DUBAD) to perform real-time and online error detection . DUBAD consists of robust and sensitive action detectors trained with different temporal range to produce inconsistencies in predictions to detect procedural and execution errors. Our experiments on three datasets show that our framework efficiently detects complex errors more effectively in real-world videos than the baselines. On the other hand, we suggest several future directions for extending this work. First, an automatic solution for finding the optimal s , l , β can make DUBAD more practical. Second, developing an architecture with explicit temporal information manipulation can provide better control over prediction inconsistency. Finally, transforming DUBAD into an online setting with a controlled delay (e.g., 3 seconds) can broaden its applicability to scenarios where higher accuracy is prioritized over real-time responsiveness.

A (summary): The paper proposes DUBAD, a real-time, online error detection framework for procedural videos that leverages prediction inconsistencies between complementary action detectors (Figure 1, Section 3.1). It ensembles two RNN-based branches with different temporal receptive fields (short s and long l), each containing a robust detector augmented by a Step Attention Module (SAM) that attends to action prototypes (Section 3.2) and a sensitive detector equipped with a Temporal-Aware Dynamic (TAD) module that applies input-dependent affine transforms with a sparsity-inducing loss to amplify sensitivity to errors (Figure 2, Section 3.3–3.4). During inference, a causal mode filter smooths predictions, and errors are flagged via majority voting over mismatches among four prediction pairs to jointly capture execution and procedural errors, including multiple errors within a video (Section 3.5). The paper provides ablations showing the effect of SAM and TAD, the majority-voting threshold, loss components, and temporal ranges s and l (Table 3, Table 5–6, Figure 5–6), and analyses illustrating how sensitive features induce predictive inconsistency on errors (Figure 3–4, Figure 8).

A (summary): 1. Clear, actionable core idea with novel operationalization. The paper turns “prediction inconsistency” into a concrete online error signal by pairing robust vs. sensitive heads and short- vs. long-term branches, then using a majority vote over four mismatch pairs (Section 3.5; Figure 1). This design directly targets both execution and procedural errors without needing ground-truth task graphs or LLM reasoning.

2. Method originality in sensitivity/robustness shaping. The Step Attention Module (SAM) uses action prototypes to stabilize robust heads (Section 3.2), while the Temporal-Aware Dynamic (TAD) module applies input-dependent affine transforms with a sparsity margin to amplify error sensitivity (Section 3.3; Eq. 3; Figure 2). The complementary roles are well-motivated and distinct.

3. Causal, online pipeline with an explicit decision rule. Training losses and inference steps are fully specified, including cross-entropy and smoothing losses (Eq. 1–2), causal mode filtering, and the mismatch-based voting rule (Section 3.4–3.5). The implementation is reproducible from the main text and figures (Figure 1–2).

4. Strong empirical validation across multiple datasets and error types. DUBAD achieves SOTA on EgoPER, Assembly-101-O, and EPIC-Tent-O (Table 1), covering execution and procedural errors. The gains are consistent across metrics (e.g., F1@10/25/50 on EgoPER; Avg-F1/E-F1/C-F1 on Assembly-101-O and EPIC-Tent-O).

5. Real-time efficiency with a lightweight model. The combined pipeline reaches 24.4 FPS with 18.8M parameters (Table 2), a practical improvement over LLM-based PREGO (1.33 FPS), and competitive despite the ensemble structure.

6. Thorough ablations that pinpoint what matters. The paper isolates the effects of SAM and TAD (Table 3), compares prediction sources for robust/sensitive votes (Table 4), evaluates the voting threshold (Table 5), and dissects loss components (Table 6). These analyses make the contribution attribution unusually clear.

7. Mechanistic evidence that sensitivity drives inconsistency on errors. Histograms (Figure 3) show sensitive heads dispersing probability mass across more classes on errors, and heatmaps (Figure 4; Figure 8) visualize feature sparsity/inconsistency induced by TAD during erroneous segments, connecting modules to behavior.

8. Demonstrated multi-error handling. Unlike prior online approaches that often stop at the first error, the majority-vote design over independent predictors naturally supports multiple and interacting errors within a video (Section 3.5; qualitative Figure 7).

9. One-class training yet robust deployment. Training exclusively on normal videos while attaining high E-F1/C-F1 (Table 1; Table 8) shows that inconsistency-based detection is effective without error supervision, addressing a key data-collection bottleneck.

10. Maintained action recognition quality in the robust heads. The robust detector retains strong temporal action segmentation performance (Table 7), indicating the method does not compromise standard recognition while adding error sensitivity.

11. Sensible temporal design backed by data analysis. The short/long temporal ranges are justified empirically with task-dependent action counts per window (Appendix Figures 12–15) and performance sweeps over s/l (Figure 6; Figure 9), supporting the dual-branch rationale.

12. Practical guidance via hyperparameter studies. The paper provides explicit sensitivity to β and voting thresholds (Figure 5; Table 5) and reports per-dataset optimal s/l/β/m (Table 12), which will help practitioners adapt the method.

A (summary): 1. Heavy per-dataset hyperparameter tuning and unclear generalization of the recipe. The method’s effectiveness hinges on carefully chosen temporal ranges (s, l), TAD margin β, and the causal mode filter m, which vary widely across datasets and even tasks (Table 12; Figure 5–6, 9–11). This undermines plug-and-play deployability for real-time assistants. Actionable: (a) report a single default configuration that performs competitively across datasets; (b) add an automatic selection strategy (e.g., validation-driven or momentum-adaptive s, l; β learned per-branch via a constraint or regularizer); (c) include sensitivity curves when deviating from the “optimal” in Table 12 to quantify robustness.

2. Limited evidence on detection latency and responsiveness. The causal mode filter is causal but uses large windows (e.g., m=150 on EPIC-Tent-O; Table 12), which likely introduces seconds of decision lag, contradicting the emphasis on instantaneous feedback. No detection delay metrics are reported. Actionable: report time-to-detect/error onset lag distributions vs. F1 on all datasets; include ablations varying m (Figure 11) together with measured latency, and add a “controlled-delay” setting as suggested in the Conclusion to characterize the accuracy–latency trade-off.

3. Error detection on EPIC-Tent-O remains weak. Despite higher Avg-F1, the error F1 is low (E-F1=27.6% with E-Precision 28.6 and E-Recall 26.7 in Table 8), suggesting limited practical utility for detecting actual mistakes in this dataset. Actionable: analyze failure modes by error type and action duration; evaluate whether tuning s/l toward longer contexts (Figure 6) or adjusting β (Figure 5/10) can improve E-Recall; consider a learned combiner (instead of hard majority vote) that weights the four pairwise inconsistencies adaptively for domains with long actions.

4. Decision rule is hand-crafted and potentially brittle. The “≥3 mismatches” threshold is selected via ablation (Table 5) but remains a hard rule over argmax labels. This discards uncertainty information in the softmax scores that could capture near-misses or partial agreement. Actionable: (a) compare against probabilistic inconsistency measures (e.g., KL/JS divergence between distributions) and calibrated entropy thresholds; (b) evaluate a light meta-classifier over the four logits pairs to learn the decision boundary; (c) consider per-branch confidence calibration to avoid overconfident but wrong sensitive predictions.

5. SAM’s reliance on fixed action prototypes may hinder out-of-distribution robustness. The Step Attention Module (Section 3.2) uses averaged per-class prototypes from normal videos, which presumes a stable action taxonomy and consistent feature semantics. There is no analysis on drift (e.g., different camera/device domains) or unseen/rare actions. Actionable: (a) add cross-domain or cross-task transfer tests (train on a subset of tasks or subjects; test on held-out ones); (b) evaluate prototype robustness to class imbalance; (c) compare to alternatives such as instance-wise memory or online-updated prototypes.

6. TAD objective lacks a clear justification for “sparsity” and selection. The TAD loss (Eq. 3) constrains the norm of Hk but is not an explicit sparsity penalty; the link to feature selection is mostly empirical via heatmaps (Figure 4, Figure 8). Actionable: (a) report quantitative sparsity metrics (e.g., proportion of near-zero channels) vs. β; (b) compare L1 vs. the current margin loss for Hk; (c) ablate the GRU inside TAD (Figure 2) to verify the necessity of temporal conditioning in producing beneficial instability.

7. Missing comparisons to simpler or broader inconsistency/uncertainty baselines. The core claim is that “inconsistency” is an effective error signal, but comparisons are limited to PREGO/DTGL and internal ablations (Table 3–6). Actionable: add baselines using (a) disagreement between only short-vs-long branches without SAM/TAD; (b) stochastic inference disagreement (e.g., dropout perturbations) or small deep ensembles; (c) entropy-based thresholds on a single robust head. This would solidify that the proposed dual-branch robust/sensitive design is necessary.

8. No reporting of variability or statistical significance. All main tables (e.g., Table 1–2) lack variance across runs/seeds. Given the small gaps at higher overlap thresholds (e.g., EgoPER F1@50 is 23.9 vs. 20.9), reproducibility is uncertain. Actionable: report mean±std over multiple seeds; for EgoPER, provide per-task/error-type breakdowns with confidence intervals.

9. Limited quantitative evaluation of multi-error scenarios. Although Figure 7 qualitatively shows multiple errors in EgoPER, there is no event-level scoring that counts how many errors were detected vs. missed, nor fragmentation/merging analysis. Actionable: add a per-error event precision/recall on EgoPER (since Assembly-101-O and EPIC-Tent-O stop at the first error) and report over-segmentation/under-segmentation rates akin to Table 9 but at the event level.

10. Feature extractor dependence and fairness. For EgoPER, features come from TimeSFormer pretrained on Ego4D; for Assembly-101-O/EPIC-Tent-O, features are those used by PREGO (Section 4.1). This mixing may confound fairness and hides the impact of the detector itself across datasets. Actionable: (a) unify the feature backbone across all datasets (at least as an additional controlled comparison); (b) report results with a lighter backbone to demonstrate robustness to feature quality and better reflect wearable-device constraints.

11. Practical deployment claims not validated on target hardware. The Introduction motivates wearable deployment (e.g., HoloLens/Vision Pro), yet runtime is only measured on an RTX A6000 (Table 2). The large smoothing windows (Table 12) also suggest non-trivial latency. Actionable: provide throughput and latency on an edge device or with mobile-class GPUs/CPUs, and include memory/energy profiles.

12. Limited error-type breakdown on EgoPER. The paper asserts coverage of nuanced execution errors (Section 1; Section 3.5), but quantitative breakdown by execution error categories (e.g., addition, modification, slip) is absent; only qualitative examples are shown (Figure 7). Actionable: add per-category metrics on EgoPER to substantiate the claim that subtle execution errors are better captured than prior online methods.
